title: The Test That Only Passes First: Shared State Between Tests

questions.question: A test fails in the suite and passes when run on its own. Where is the defect most likely to be?
options: In a test that ran earlier and changed something the failing test depends on
In the failing test, since that is the one reporting
In the test framework, which must be reporting the wrong name
Nowhere: a test that passes alone is a passing test
questions.explanation: The failing test is the victim, not the culprit. Something outside it survived the test before it, and the one that reports is simply the one downstream of the leak.

questions.question: Two probes share one double. The first dirties it, the second expects the default. Forwards they score 1 of 2. What do they score backwards, and why?
options: 2 of 2, because the one expecting the default now runs before anything has dirtied it
1 of 2, because the same probe is still broken whichever way they run
0 of 2, because reversing the order breaks both of them
2 of 2, because running a suite backwards resets the values it touches
questions.explanation: Measured in this lesson: 1 forwards and 2 backwards. Leaked state flows forward, so reversing moves the victim in front of the culprit and it passes.

questions.question: Why does Restore put the value back in a destructor rather than on the last line of the test?
options: An early return, a failed check, a break or a throw all skip a line at the end, and none of them skip a destructor
A destructor runs faster than an assignment at the end of a function
Because the last line of a test is reserved for the assertion
So the value can be restored more than once if the test needs it
questions.explanation: This is lesson 02-03's point applied to tests. The paths that most need the cleanup are exactly the paths that do not reach the bottom of the function.

questions.question: Restore declares a destructor, which lesson 03-09 said suppresses the implicit move and is usually worth avoiding. Why is it right here?
options: A guard that could be moved could restore twice or not at all, so copy and move are deleted deliberately
Scope guards are exempt because they are small
The rule of zero applies only to types that own memory
Templates cannot have implicit move operations anyway
questions.explanation: The rule of zero is a default, not a law. Knowing a rule includes knowing the cases where it stops applying, and a one-shot guard is one of them.

questions.question: The first version of run_in_both_orders had no reset between its two passes. With a known leaky pair it reported 1 forwards and 0 backwards, and the test asserting order dependence still passed. What was wrong?
options: The backwards pass inherited the dirty value from the forwards pass, so both probes failed, and the counts were untrue even though they differed
Nothing: 1 and 0 differ, so the detection was correct
The loop ran off the end of the vector when counting down
The reset should have been called once, after both passes
questions.explanation: A tool for finding shared state had shared state between its own two passes. The assertion held for the wrong reason, and only printing the numbers and reading them caught it.

questions.question: Running a suite in both orders and getting equal counts proves what?
options: That these two orders agree, which is weaker than no leak and much stronger than one order
That the suite has no shared state between its tests
Nothing at all, since two orders out of n! is negligible
That the tests can safely be run in parallel
questions.explanation: Only every permutation would be a proof and there are too many. Reversing catches the common case because leaks flow forward, for the cost of running the suite twice.
